sections.learningObjectives:
- Identify common medical word roots and their meanings.
- Explain combining forms and the combining vowel.
- Decode unfamiliar terms by their roots.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Cardi/o is a code word for the heart. If you hear "cardiac," it is always about the heart, like a cardiac nurse who helps heart patients.

### Question 2

Gastr/o means stomach. When you eat a big meal, your "gastric" juices in your stomach help break the food down.

### Question 3

Hepat/o means liver. "Hepatitis" is when the liver gets swollen and angry, and it starts with the same "hepat" sound.

### Question 4

Nephr/o means kidney. A "nephrologist" is a doctor who takes care of kidneys, which clean your blood like a filter.

### Question 5

Oste/o means bone. Your bones are your body's frame, and words like "osteoporosis" tell us the frame is getting weaker.

### Question 6

Arthr/o means joint — the places where your bones bend, like your knee or elbow. "Arthritis" is when those bendy spots get sore and swollen.

### Question 7

My/o means muscle. Your muscles are what let you run and lift things, and "myalgia" just means your muscles are sore.

### Question 8

Neur/o means nerve. Nerves are the body's message wires that carry signals to and from your brain.

### Question 9

Dermat/o means skin. A "dermatologist" is the skin doctor — the person you see for rashes and bumps.

### Question 10

Hemat/o means blood. A "hematoma" is a bruise — blood that has leaked and pooled under your skin.

### Question 11

Ophthalm/o means eye. An "ophthalmologist" is an eye doctor — the long word is just the eye's fancy name.

### Question 12

Ot/o means ear. An "otoscope" is the little light tool a doctor uses to peek inside your ear.

### Question 13

Rhin/o means nose. A "rhinoceros" has a big horn on its nose — same word clue!

### Question 14

Most medical words use the letter "o" as a glue sound, like gastr-o. It is just the most comfortable sound to say between two word parts.

### Question 15

A combining form is like a LEGO brick with a connector already on it. The word root is the brick, and the vowel "o" is the little connector that helps it snap onto other bricks.

### Question 16

The "o" is there so words do not sound bumpy. Saying "gastr-enter-itis" is awkward, but "gastroenteritis" rolls right off the tongue.

### Question 17

If the next piece starts with a consonant (like "-logy"), you keep the "o" as a bridge so the word is easy to say: gastro-logy.

### Question 18

When the next piece starts with a vowel (like "-itis"), you drop the "o" so you do not get two vowels bumping together. Gastr + itis = gastritis.

### Question 19

The "o" is just glue between two word parts. Gastr-o-enter-o-logy strings "stomach" and "intestine" together so you can say the word smoothly.

### Question 20

Cardi/o is the "heart brick with a connector." The "-logy" on the end means "the study of," so cardiology is the study of the heart.

### Question 21

The root is the core idea — "gastr" means stomach. The "-itis" at the end means inflammation, so gastritis is a sore, inflamed stomach.

### Question 22

A combining form is written with a slash between the root and its vowel, like gastr/o. The slash is just a reminder that the "o" is a connector, not part of the root.

### Question 23

Think of a combining form as the main ingredient and a suffix as the instruction at the end. "Gastr/o" (stomach) + "-itis" (inflammation) = an inflamed stomach.

### Question 24

Cardiology = "heart" + "study of." So a cardiologist is a heart doctor.

### Question 25

Gastr = stomach and -itis = inflammation. Gastritis is an irritated, sore stomach lining.

### Question 26

Hepat = liver and -itis = inflammation. Hepatitis means a swollen, irritated liver.

### Question 27

Nephr = kidney and -itis = inflammation. Nephritis is when a kidney is inflamed.

### Question 28

Arthr = joint and -itis = inflammation. Arthritis is a sore, swollen joint.

### Question 29

Ot = ear and -itis = inflammation. Otitis is an ear infection — the earache kids often get.

### Question 30

Dermat = skin and -itis = inflammation. Dermatitis is red, itchy, irritated skin.

### Question 31

Rhin = nose and -itis = inflammation. Rhinitis is a stuffy, runny, irritated nose — like with allergies.

### Question 32

My/o = muscle and -algia = pain. Myalgia is just the medical word for sore, aching muscles.

### Question 33

Neur = nerve and -itis = inflammation. Neuritis is a nerve that is swollen and sore.

### Question 34

Enter = intestine and -itis = inflammation. Enteritis is an angry, inflamed intestine.

### Question 35

Col = colon and -itis = inflammation. Colitis is an irritated large intestine.

### Question 36

Angi/o means blood tube. An "angiogram" is a picture of the body's blood tubes (vessels) to check for blockages.

### Question 37

Encephal/o = brain and -pathy = disease. Encephalopathy means the brain is not working the way it should.

### Question 38

Ophthalm/o = eye and -logist = specialist. An ophthalmologist is an eye doctor.

### Question 39

Hyster/o = uterus and -ectomy = cutting out. A hysterectomy is surgery to remove the uterus.

### Question 40

Mamm/o = breast and -gram = picture. A mammogram is a special picture of the breast that helps find problems early.

### Question 41

Aden/o = gland and -oma = growth/tumor. An adenoma is a usually harmless lump that grows from gland tissue.

### Question 42

Hist/o = tissue and -logy = study of. Histology is looking at thin slices of tissue under a microscope.

### Question 43

Cyt/o = cell and -logy = study of. Cytology is examining individual cells, like the cells in a Pap test.

### Question 44

Path/o = disease and -logy = study of. A pathology report tells what a doctor found when they studied tissue or fluid for signs of disease.

### Question 45

Carcin/o = cancer. A "carcinoma" is a cancer — cells growing out of control in the body's lining tissues.

### Question 46

Onc/o = tumor or mass. An "oncologist" is a doctor who treats tumors, whether they are harmless or cancer.

### Question 47

Hepato = liver and -megaly = too big. So hepatomegaly means a liver that has grown larger than normal.

### Question 48

Nephrology = kidney + study of. A nephrologist is a kidney doctor.

### Question 49

Neur = nerve and -logy = study of. Neurology is all about the brain, spinal cord, and nerves.

### Question 50

Leuko = white and -cyte = cell. Leukocytes are your white blood cells that fight off germs.

### Question 51

Erythro = red and -cyte = cell. Erythrocytes are the red blood cells that carry oxygen around your body.

### Question 52

Melan/o means black or dark. "Melanoma" is a serious skin cancer named for the dark color of the cells involved.

### Question 53

Cyan/o means blue. "Cyanosis" is when skin or lips turn bluish because the body is not getting enough oxygen.

### Question 54

Therm/o means heat. "Hyperthermia" means the body has gotten too hot — the opposite of being too cold.

### Question 55

Cry/o means cold. "Cryotherapy" uses freezing cold to treat things like warts or sore muscles.

### Question 56

Py/o = pus and -uria = in the urine. Pyuria means pus in the pee, a sign of a urinary infection.

### Question 57

Hydr/o means water. "Dehydration" means your body is low on water — like a plant that needs a drink.

### Question 58

Lip/o means fat. "Lipids" are fats in your blood that doctors check to keep your heart healthy.

### Question 59

Glyc/o = sugar and hypo- = too little. Hypoglycemia means your blood sugar is too low.

### Question 60

Nephr/o = kidney and lith/o = stone. Nephrolithiasis is the medical word for kidney stones — hard little rocks that form in the kidneys.

### Question 61

Splen/o = spleen and -megaly = too big. Splenomegaly means the spleen has grown larger than normal.

### Question 62

Pneum/o means lung or air. "Pneumonia" is when the lungs get sick and inflamed, making it hard to breathe.

### Question 63

Cephal/o = head and -algia = pain. Cephalalgia is just the medical word for a headache.

### Question 64

Gastroenteritis strings together "stomach" and "intestines" plus "inflammation." It is the fancy word for a tummy bug.

### Question 65

Cyst/o means bladder (the body's pee bag). "Cystitis" means that bag is inflamed — a bladder infection.

### Question 66

Cholecyst/o means gallbladder — the little sac that stores bile to help digest fat. A "cholecystectomy" is surgery to take it out.

### Question 67

Gloss/o means tongue. "Glossitis" means the tongue is sore or swollen.

### Question 68

Osteoarthritis is built from "bone" + "joint" + "inflammation." It is the wear-and-tear arthritis that affects joints.

### Question 69

Electrocardiogram = electricity + heart + picture. It draws a picture of the electricity that makes your heart beat.

### Question 70

Hepatorenal mixes "hepato" (liver) and "renal" (kidney) into one word. If you know both roots, you know it is about the liver and kidneys working together.

### Question 71

Xanth/o means yellow. A "xanthoma" is a yellowish lump under the skin that can be a sign of high cholesterol.

### Question 72

Poli/o means gray. "Polio" is short for poliomyelitis — an illness that harmed the gray part of the spinal cord.

### Question 73

Scler/o means hard. "Arteriosclerosis" is when the blood tubes (arteries) get hard and stiff, which is bad for the heart.

### Question 74

Sten/o means narrow. "Stenosis" is when a tube in the body, like a blood vessel or the spine's canal, becomes too narrow.

### Question 75

Chondr/o means cartilage — the smooth cushion between bones. "Chondromalacia" means that cushion has gotten soft and weak.
